title: r/longevity on Reddit: Exploring the effects of Dasatinib, Quercetin, and Fisetin on DNA methylation clocks: a longitudinal study on senolytic interventions
abstract:

Remarkably, the addition of Fisetin to the treatment resulted in non-significant increases in epigenetic age acceleration, suggesting a potential mitigating effect of Fisetin on the impact of DQ on epigenetic aging. Whether you believe epi clocks are measuring something meaningful about biological age or not, senolytics continue to underwhelm in humans and this is consistent with the failure of fisetin in the NIA ITP lifespan studies
See eg https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2023/09/a-continued-painfully-slow-assessment-of-the-dasatinib-and-quercetin-senolytic-treatment-in-human-trials/ but I know his optimism is also based not only on published studies but also on many anecdotal reports of n=1 use by people (including himself). (c) Kirkland says that ITP failure of fisetin is because Miller refused to heed his advice on how to run the trial.
None of this is a reason to be skeptical of next-gen senolytics currently in pre-clinical development by a half dozen+ companies. I still have high hopes for several companies that are marching steadily towards clinical trials. (The 3 I'm personally invested in all still seem great based on all data generated so far: Rubedo, Oisin, & Deciduous.) Last I checked fisetin was regarded as one of the most promising compounds, even over D + Q, for senolytic activity from prior pubs from Kirkland himself.
Miller has already delivered a critique that to me is crippling for the foundational paper by Campisi that the whole CS/senolytics field has been built upon. He talks about it in his recent talk with Peter Attia, highly recommend it if you haven't watched it · c) Kirkland says that ITP failure of fisetin is because Miller refused to heed his advice on how to run the trial.
